title: Why You Must Display Your Classroom Management Plan
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a visible, posted classroom management plan is a diagnostic he uses when walking into classrooms because it signals how much importance a teacher places on protecting learning from disruption. He lays out six distinct functions a posted plan serves beyond simple record-keeping: it sends a message to everyone entering the room that learning is sacred, it acts as a neutral reference point during behavior conversations, it reminds students that misbehavior is a choice while enforcement is a promise kept, it puts the teacher on notice to follow their own rules, it makes a public statement of willingness to hold students accountable, and it declares clear behavioral expectations to the world. The concrete recommendation is to write or print rules and consequences on easel-size paper or poster board and mount it high on the front wall, so that anyone who sees it thinks the teacher means business.
points: A posted classroom management plan functions as a public symbol of trust, fairness, and objectivity that students can point back to.
The plan should be printed on easel-size paper or poster board and mounted high on the front wall, not tucked away.
Posting the plan puts the teacher on notice too, since it commits them publicly to following through on what they've displayed.
The absence of a posted plan is one of the first things Linsin looks for when evaluating how seriously a teacher protects learning time.
quotes: When I visit classrooms, I rarely see a classroom management plan posted. It’s the first thing I look for.
Because it tells me a lot about the teacher. Namely, the importance they place on protecting students from disruptions in learning.
Rules and consequences posted high on the wall of your classroom send the message to everyone who enters—students, parents, and administrators alike—that learning is sacred.
A poster of your plan is a reminder to students that misbehavior is a choice they make, while enforcement is the fulfillment of a promise you made.
With your plan out in the open for all to see, you’re put on notice. You can’t escape it. It whispers to you throughout every day that you’re obligated to follow it.
I recommend writing or printing out your rules and consequences on easel-size paper or poster board and affixing it high on the front wall of your classroom.
